about: A PROJECT-DEFINED EDITORIAL EQUIVALENT, NOT AN EXTERNAL SYLLABUS. NOTHING IN THIS FILE MAY BE ATTRIBUTED TO ANY TELUGU EXAMINING OR LANGUAGE BODY -- not to Potti Sreeramulu Telugu University, not to the Telugu Akademi, not to any state or diaspora examination -- and nothing in it may be attributed to DELE, the Instituto Cervantes or the Plan Curricular ABOUT TELUGU. Unlike Hindi, which has a named external ladder to disclaim, and Marathi, which has a government-employee examination to disclaim, Telugu has NO named external ladder at all, so there is no body whose syllabus this could be confused with. That absence is the disclaimer. Three claims are stacked here and they have very different strengths, so read them apart. (1) THE POINT SET is derived structurally from core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json, which restates the A1 grammar, function, notion and orthography inventories the Instituto Cervantes publishes behind DELE -- a real awarding body with a published syllabus, finite and split into A1 and A2 columns. That is the strongest thing in this file, and all it establishes is a LEVEL: what an A1 candidate must be able to handle, asked as a language-neutral demand rather than as a piece of Spanish grammar. (2) THE TELUGU EXPONENTS are editorial throughout and are this project's judgement and nobody else's. Deciding that Spanish's personal `a` is answered by Telugu's accusative -ni, that its `gustar` frame is answered by the dative-subject sentence, or that its four article points are answered by the single fact that Telugu has no article, is a choice made here. ATTRIBUTE NOTHING IN THIS FILE TO DELE OR THE INSTITUTO CERVANTES ABOUT TELUGU: they published a Spanish syllabus and have said nothing whatever about this language. (3) THE COVERAGE NUMBER this file produces is a measure of the corpus against this list. It is not an exam-readiness claim, and it cannot become one while every scope dimension is `partial`. WHY A PROXY AT ALL: no awarding body publishes a content syllabus for Telugu. core/exam-levels.json records this track as exam 'no widely-sat ladder', basis 'editorial', mapping 'cefr', with no caveat at all -- the barest entry of any Indic track in that file -- and that was re-read before this file was written. The parallel Hindi and Marathi inventories settled the wider negative result already and it is not repeated here: there is no South Asian equivalent of the Plan Curricular, and the Council of Europe has issued no Reference Level Description for any language of the region. WHAT THIS FILE DOES NOT CLAIM, stated plainly because the omission matters: no fresh external search for a Telugu awarding body was carried out for this file, and that was a DECISION rather than an omission. BACKLOG.d HL-C287 and HL-C290 record the search as settled and instruct in as many words: the Hindi tranche ran the sourcing question against the best-placed South Asian candidate and came back empty, there is no South Asian PCIC, and no further agent-hours are to be spent hunting one for another Indic track. This file follows that instruction and states the consequence rather than hiding it: if a Telugu syllabus does exist, this file has not ruled it out. THE EVIDENCE BASE HERE IS THINNER THAN HINDI'S OR MARATHI'S, AND THAT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT THING TO KNOW ABOUT IT. Hindi's inventory could pin exponents against two checked-in timed A1 mocks; Marathi's could pin them against the eleven paper parts of task-shapes/a1.json. Telugu has NEITHER. There is no telugu/assessment-spec.md, no telugu/task-shapes/ and no telugu/mocks/ -- the directory holds lessons, chapters, curriculum, narration, a roadmap, a session map and a pronunciation reference, and nothing that fixes what an A1 paper would ask. Every exponent choice below is therefore bounded by the proxy alone, with no project-internal contract to check it against. Writing that contract is the single change that would most improve this file. PROXY ACCOUNTING: every one of the proxy's 273 points is accounted for. 268 are cited by some point's `derivedFrom`; the remaining 5 are named here as untransferable, with the reason: A1-O1-04: capital letters -- the Telugu script is unicameral and has no case distinction to teach. A1-O1-05: initial lower-case letters -- same reason. A1-O1-06: superscript letters in frequent abbreviations -- a Spanish typographic convention with no Telugu counterpart. A1-O2-01: the general rules of written accentuation -- Telugu writes no accent; vowel length is carried by a separate sign, which TE-A1-L-05 covers instead. A1-O2-02: the diacritic tilde that separates el from el -- no Telugu counterpart. Points marked `telugu-specific` in `derivedFrom` answer no Spanish demand at all -- the suffixing morphology, the two-way negative, the dative-subject family, the self-benefactive -koo, suppletion in `raa`, the five-taste set and the register judgements on the time-of-day greetings. A proxy is a scaffold, not a template to translate, and those are why. LEVEL PURITY IS NOT A CONSTRAINT ON THIS CURRICULUM, so a point is recorded as covered when the corpus teaches it, whether or not the corpus teaches it at A1: the sixteen body-part atoms and the thirteen kinship atoms are both well past A1 and both count.
source: PROJECT-DEFINED. LEVEL PROXY: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json, the DELE/PCIC-sourced Spanish A1 point set, used for the STRUCTURE of what an A1 learner must handle. Its own source is https://cvc.cervantes.es/ensenanza/biblioteca_ele/plan_curricular/niveles/02_gramatica_inventario_a1-a2.htm and the sibling function, notion and orthography inventories. Nothing about Telugu is attributed to DELE, the Instituto Cervantes or the Plan Curricular. EXAM ENVELOPE: NONE EXISTS. Unlike hindi/assessment-spec.md with hindi/task-shapes/a1.json and hindi/mocks/a1/, and unlike marathi/assessment-spec.md with marathi/task-shapes/a1.json, the telugu track ships no assessment spec, no task shapes and no mocks, so no project-internal contract bounds the exponent choices or the gap notes in this file. PROFICIENCY BACKBONE: core/exam-levels.json, tracks.telugu -- exam 'no widely-sat ladder', basis 'editorial', mapping 'cefr'. CORPUS EVIDENCE: every probe was checked mechanically against the atoms declared by the 301 lesson files in code/learning/human-languages/telugu/lessons/, which introduce 404 distinct atoms between them. The script points' counts were taken from the 49 script-recognition lessons in that same directory, one glyph each, and the letter inventory they are compared against is the Telugu block of Unicode as set out in telugu/pronunciation-reference.md. NOT SEARCHED, BY INSTRUCTION: no external search for a Telugu awarding-body syllabus was performed for this file. code/learning/human-languages/BACKLOG.d/02610-HL-C287-USE-SPANISH-AS-A-LEVEL-PROXY-WHEN-A-TRACK-HAS-NO-SYL-f1667cbc.md and 02610-HL-C290-ANCHORING-AN-EXAM-INVENTORY-WHEN-NO-SYLLABUS-EXISTS-b3f27a1e.md record that search as settled and direct that it not be repeated per track. See `about`.

communicative-functions.note: The proxy's functional column is finite and level-split, which is what would close a dimension -- for Spanish. It does not close this one, and here the shortfall is worse than in the parallel Hindi file: the exponent realising each function in Telugu is our choice every time, and unlike Hindi there is no checked-in mock item anywhere in the track that pins one down. All 54 proxy function points are answered, plus seven the proxy has no A1 slot for -- the register judgements on the greetings, the -andi politeness ending, and the household-visit courtesy formulas. The sixty-one points here are the least externally anchored in the file.

grammar.source: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json (the proxy's grammar, sentence and coordination columns)
grammar.note: THE DIMENSION THE PROXY HELPS MOST AND STILL DOES NOT CLOSE. No published Telugu equivalent of the PCIC grammar inventory exists, and with no mocks to mine, the proxy is the only thing bounding this column at all. Walking it surfaced demands a reading of the lessons alone would not have raised: the article points surfaced that nothing tells a learner Telugu HAS no article; the personal-`a` point surfaced the missing accusative -ni; the full-paradigm verb point surfaced that four of Telugu's six persons are never taught. It does not close, because a demand Spanish does not make can still be an A1 demand in Telugu -- the mahat/amahat noun class, the quotative `ani` and the relative participle are the obvious ones -- and nothing bounds those.

phonology-orthography.source: The Telugu block of Unicode for the letter inventory, telugu/pronunciation-reference.md for the sound system, and code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json for the orthographic demands
phonology-orthography.note: Two halves in very different states, and it is worth saying so rather than quietly averaging them. The SCRIPT half is nearly closed, because Telugu's letter inventory is finite and enumerable: the script points state exactly which letters have a recognition lesson and which do not, and the notes give the counts -- 23 of about 36 consonants, 4 of about 12 independent vowels, 10 of 12 everyday vowel signs, and all 10 digits. WHAT 'HAS NO LESSON' MEANS HERE, AND WHY IT DOES NOT CONTRADICT THE SCRIPT-CLOSURE GATE: the track's 301 lesson files use 64 distinct Telugu characters and 49 of them have a dedicated recognition lesson declaring an atom of their own. The other 15 are taught only inside a word, which is what `script-closure.ts` counts, and why that gate correctly reports telugu with ZERO never-taught glyphs. This inventory asks the narrower question a probe can answer -- does the letter have an atom -- and for those 15 it does not. The occurrence counts in the script notes were measured over those same 301 files, not estimated: ma 636, retroflex ta 292, independent a 248, the oo sign 211, ba 169, the o sign 144. The two measurements are asking different questions and both answers are right. The PRONUNCIATION half is closed against measurement rather than complete: the track's sound material lives in per-lesson `sounds:` front matter and in pronunciation-reference.md, and NEITHER declares an atom, so no probe can reach either and all seven points are unmapped for a structural reason rather than because nothing is taught. Drawing an A1/A2 line through Telugu phonology ourselves would be the editorial promotion the Spanish file itself declines to make, so this stays partial.

lexicon.source: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json (the proxy's 36 general-notion and 77 specific-notion A1 points)
lexicon.note: No published A1 Telugu word list exists -- no awarding-body list, no Goethe-style Wortliste, no ranked frequency band adopted by anybody. What the proxy supplies is a bounded set of DOMAINS, which is a real improvement on domains chosen by us, and walking it is what showed that this track's lexis is shaped by a village and a household rather than by a city and a transaction: fauna, flora, tools, kitchen, body and kinship are richly covered, while transport, media, leisure, documents and payment have nothing at all. It does not close, because the proxy bounds the domains and never the words inside one, and because the domain list is Spanish-shaped: it has no slot for the five-taste set or for the courtesy abstractions this track teaches.

probeSemantics: A point counts as COVERED when every atom in `probe` is introduced by some lesson in the track. `probe: null` means no atom in the corpus corresponds to this point, which is itself the finding -- an unmapped point is uncovered, never skipped. Every atom named in every probe was checked mechanically against the atoms the telugu track actually introduces, by re-reading the 301 lesson files; a probe naming an atom that does not exist would report 'not covered' forever and be indistinguishable from real debt, so an id was never invented to fill a point. Where the corpus cannot demonstrate a point it gets `probe: null` and a note saying what is missing. ONE HABIT IS NAMED HERE SO IT IS NOT A HIDDEN GENEROSITY: several chapters declare no LEX atom at all and carry only ETYMON, PRAGMATICS or SCRIPT atoms -- C09 (sorry), C10 (the weekdays), C15 (water and rice), C20 (the teens, and the weather), C21, C22 (green and yellow), C23 to C30 (the parts of the day). Probing those points therefore names an etymology or pragmatics atom rather than a lexis one. The word IS introduced by that lesson; the track simply files it under a different atom kind, and every such probe says so in its note. A point is NOT counted as covered when only part of what it names is taught: `manci` without an antonym leaves general evaluation uncovered, `taruvaata` without `mundu` leaves the before/after contrast uncovered, and the six body-part chapters do not buy any credit for physical description. That is deliberate, because a candidate asked for the other half of a pair gets no partial credit. `derivedFrom` records each point's provenance -- the proxy point ids whose demand it answers, or `telugu-specific` -- and is carried for auditability; no code reads it. CHAPTERS 74-80 UPDATE: a vocabulary tranche of 35 headwords was authored against this file's own uncovered list, and 44 points moved from `probe: null` to a probe. Eight more moved only PARTLY and kept `probe: null` with the note rewritten to say what landed and what did not -- half a pair buys nothing here, which is the rule this file started with and did not bend to make its own number larger. Every word in that tranche is spelled from characters the corpus already used, so no point was closed at the cost of new script debt; TE-A1-DEM-03 records the one point that could not be closed for exactly that reason.

points.label: proper nouns: a personal name, dropped into the frame that carries it
points.note: The frame `naa peru X` is taught and is exactly the slot a name goes in, but no Telugu personal name is itself an atom: the lesson's `Arun` is an example inside the prose.

points.label: forms of address: the respectful -garu suffixed to a name
place names: the town, district or state you live in, and the country
points.note: PARTLY CLOSED, WHICH IS NOT CLOSED. C77 introduces `bhaaratadeesam` (India), the track's first proper place name, along with `pattanam` (a town) and `deesam` (a country). The point also asks for the town, district or state you LIVE IN, and no settlement or state has a name here yet, so the probe stays null. TE-A1-X-10, which asks only that you can say where you are from, IS now covered.

points.label: common nouns naming periods of time
noun class: the mahat / amahat (human / non-human) split that drives agreement
points.note: Telugu's counterpart to Spanish gender, and never stated. The track introduces five -du nouns whose class is precisely what -du marks (snehitudu, vaidyudu, alludu, suuryudu, candrudu) and says nothing about the category.

points.label: gender by heteronymy: separate words for the male and the female of a pair
number: forming the plural of a noun with -lu / -alu, as a rule a learner can apply
points.note: Two atoms come close and neither states the rule. C01's agglutination lens says a plural rides on `dhanyavaadamulu`; C18's time lens shows `ganta` becoming `gantalu` past one o'clock. A candidate is shown two plural forms and never told how to make a third.

points.label: the stem change a noun undergoes before a case ending
points.note: C79's genitive lesson states the stem change directly: the ending never lands on the dictionary form, the noun leans toward it first.

points.label: verbal nouns: one form serving as both the verb and its noun
qualifying adjectives in attributive use, standing before the noun
the adjective never changes: no agreement for gender, number or case
points.note: Spanish spends two A1 points on adjective agreement. The Telugu answer is that there is none, and C42 states it in as many words -- one of the few places the track answers a proxy demand head on.

points.label: predicative use: an adjective as the whole comment, with the -di / -vaadu ending it needs
relational adjectives: saying which place or people someone belongs to
points.note: No gentilic, no country name and no -vaadu / -vaallu derivation. Spanish's `espanol` has no counterpart a candidate could produce.

points.label: degree: 'very' with an adjective
the everyday size and age adjectives: big, small, new, old
Telugu has no article: a bare noun is definite or indefinite from context alone
points.note: The largest structural difference from the proxy language, and the track never states it. Spanish spends four A1 points on the article; a learner arriving from English needs telling once that Telugu has none and what does the work instead.

points.label: `oka` before a noun as the nearest thing Telugu has to 'a'
points.note: `okati` is taught as the numeral one (C07) and `oka ganta` appears in C18's clock lens as 'one o'clock'. Neither teaches `oka` as an indefinite marker, which is a different job.

points.label: pointing at a definite thing with idi / adi
the i- / a- / e- system: one slot changes and gives near, far and question
spatial deixis: here and there
the demonstrative used before its noun (ii pustakam, aa manishi)
points.note: STILL UNCOVERED, AND THE REASON IS THE SCRIPT. The adnominal pair is `ii` and `aa`, and `ii` is written with the independent vowel letter EE (U+0C08), which occurs ZERO times anywhere in the track. Teaching it would add a glyph the corpus has never shown and raise `script-closure` from zero, so the C74-C80 tranche spelled every one of its 35 words from characters already in use and left this point alone. Closing it needs a script lesson for that letter first, not a vocabulary lesson.

points.label: two spatial degrees, not Spanish's three
points.note: The proxy's three-way este/ese/aquel does not transfer: C41's lens sets out three beginnings of which only two are spatial, the third being the question word.

points.label: naa / nii / mii before the noun
possessives with several possessors: our (inclusive and exclusive), your, their
points.note: Two of the three persons. C79 teaches `maa` and `mana`, the exclusive and inclusive `our`, which is the split Spanish does not even make; `mii` for the plural your was already taught at C02. `vaari`, their, is still not introduced, so the probe stays null.

points.label: the genitive on a full noun, not just a pronoun
a possessive standing alone: 'this one is mine'
cardinal numerals one to ten
cardinal numerals eleven to twenty
points.note: C20 carries only etymon atoms, so this probe names an etymology atom rather than a lexis one. That is the only atom the lesson offers; the teens are genuinely taught.

points.label: cardinals above twenty: the tens and the hundreds, which prices and ages need
points.note: C77 teaches the tens 30 to 90 and `vanda` 100 in one lesson, the way C07 taught one to five.

points.label: ordinal numerals to tenth
relative quantity: a little, more, less
'enough', closing a quantity negotiation
degree words: very, quite, a bit, modifying a quantity
the Telugu digits, read as quantities
points.note: All ten digit glyphs have a lesson each -- the one part of the writing system the track finishes.

points.label: measures: size, distance and weight, with a unit
points.note: `tuukam` ('weight', C72) is the only measure noun and no unit -- kilo, metre, rupee, hour of distance -- is introduced beside it.

points.label: grammar is suffixes: Telugu glues endings onto a stem, one after another
points.note: No Spanish counterpart. It is the single fact that makes the rest of Telugu morphology legible, and the track states it in Chapter 1.

points.label: the dative -ku, 'to / for'
the locative -loo, 'in', for saying where you live
the accusative -ni / -nu, which a human object takes and a thing does not
the comitative -too, 'with'
the ablative `nunchi`, 'from', which saying where you come from needs
sandhi: an ending fusing onto the noun in front of it
points.note: Spanish's `a + el = al` is a contraction rule; Telugu's counterpart is regular vowel sandhi, and C19 shows it fusing `nii vayasu` + `enta` into `nii vayasenta`.

points.label: the relational word follows its noun: Telugu postposes where English preposes
the shape of every finite verb: stem, then tense piece, then person ending
one tense piece -ta- covering both 'I go' and 'I will go'
the progressive -tunnaa-, 'I am going right now'
the past piece -aa-, 'I went'
points.note: One atom carries three proxy points because C32's table sets the three tense pieces out together. The past is shown for two verbs and never generalised to a paradigm.

points.label: the person endings: -nu for I, -aaru for you-respectful
no gender on the first or second person: a man and a woman say the same word
the subject pronoun can be dropped because the ending carries it
undu / unnaanu: existing, staying and being somewhere
the zero copula: 'my name is X' has no verb in it
points.note: Spanish spends two A1 points distinguishing ser from estar. The Telugu demand behind them is the opposite one -- noticing that the verb is absent -- and C02 meets it directly.

points.label: undu has no negative, so lee- is fetched from another verb to supply one
the respectful command in -andi
the plain command: the bare stem, to someone you address as nuvvu
suppletion: the word you name the verb by is not the word the endings attach to
points.note: Spanish's irregular preterites are the nearest demand. Telugu's version is sharper: raa- takes no endings at all and vaccu supplies every form.

points.label: the stem's middle vowel moving between forms (cadu- / cadi- / cada-)
the participle chain: 'having gone, I come'
noun + ceeyu makes a new verb, which is how most borrowed vocabulary becomes verbal
the self-benefactive -koo, Telugu's answer to the reflexive
the personless verb telusu, where the knower rides in the dative instead
the infinitive: a non-finite form a candidate can build and use
points.note: The track names verbs by their stem (vellu, tinu, caduvu) and never teaches the -adam / -ataniki forms that make a verb usable as a complement.

points.label: the past participle and the perfect
the habitual past: what you used to do
the third person endings: he, she, it, they
two negatives: leedu for existence, kaadu for identity, and choosing between them
points.note: A demand Spanish does not make -- `no` covers both -- and one the track meets carefully in Chapter 1.

points.label: leedu negating existence inside a sentence
negating an ordinary verb: 'I do not go'
eemiti, 'what'
evaru, 'who'
ekkada, 'where'
elaa, 'how'
enta, 'how much' -- the price question and the age question
eppudu, 'when'
enduku, 'why', and answering it
points.note: Both halves: `enduku` asks and `endukantee` answers, which is what the point demands. The e- question row is complete with C75's `eppudu`.

points.label: the yes-or-no question: the -aa particle, or the same sentence said with a rise
the question word sits where its answer sits, not at the front of the sentence
place deictics: ikkada and akkada
time deictics forward: now, tomorrow, the day after tomorrow
points.note: `reepu` is introduced inside the whole farewell `reepu kaluddaam`, which is the atom that carries it.

points.label: time deictics backward and present: today and yesterday
quantity adverbs: koncem, ekkuva, takkuva
manner: baagaa, 'well', and its use as the answer to 'how are you'
polarity: avunu and leedu as one-word answers
connective adverbs: 'also' and 'only'
'still' and 'after that', ordering two things in a reply
word order: the verb comes last
points.note: Every example sentence in the track is verb-final and no atom says so. A candidate is given the pattern by exposure and never given the rule, which is what a production task needs.

points.label: the plain affirmative declarative
the attributive sentence, which in Telugu has no verb at all
the existential sentence: there is, there is not
the dative-subject sentence: the experiencer is not the grammatical subject
points.note: Spanish reaches the same shape only through `gustar`. Telugu runs four sentence types on it -- a skill, a fact, a meaning that landed and a taste -- and C34's lens sets all four side by side.

points.label: the transitive sentence with an unmarked direct object
the vocative: calling or hailing somebody
subject-verb agreement, stated as a rule rather than left to be noticed
noun-phrase complements: an adjective, a genitive and a relative clause
points.note: The adjective slot is taught (C42); the genitive is taught only on pronouns; the relative participle is absent entirely. A point needs all three to be true and only one is.

points.label: 'and': joining two nouns or two clauses
'or', which offering a choice needs
'but', which qualifying anything needs
negative coordination: neither this nor that
distributive coordination: one... the other
'in that case', linking a reply to what was just said
sequencing two events with 'after that'
a finite clause as object: 'I think that...', with the quotative ani
a non-finite clause as subject or object
a relative clause, which Telugu builds with a participle and not a pronoun
a causal clause: because
a purpose clause: in order to
simultaneity: when
points.note: C75 teaches `eppudu` as the QUESTION word `when?`. The subordinating `when` this point asks for is a different form (-appudu on the verb, or -tee), and no lesson teaches it.

points.label: neenu, 'I'
nuvvu and miiru, and respect carried by the plural
the rest of the paradigm: we (two kinds), he, she, they
points.note: The four missing persons in two lessons: `maa`/`mana` for the two kinds of we, and `atanu`/`aame`/`vaallu` for the third person.

points.label: the object form of a pronoun: 'see me', 'ask him'
naaku: the pronoun in the dative, as the experiencer of a state
idi and adi standing in for a thing already mentioned
a pronoun carrying a case ending (naa + ku = naaku)
the exclamative: 'how good!'
the seven weekdays
points.note: C10 carries no lexis atom, so the probe names the etymology and pragmatics atoms the lesson does declare.

points.label: the twelve months
points.note: The months taught are the lunisolar Caitram-to-Phaalgunam set. They are real Telugu months and they are NOT the names a form field, a ticket or a date of birth uses, which are the Gregorian ones -- so this point is covered and the writing task behind it still is not.

points.label: the four seasons
the parts of the day: morning, noon, afternoon, evening, night, midnight
points.note: Eight chapters (C17, C23-C31) are spent on this one notion, which is the deepest single thing the track teaches.

points.label: telling the clock time
points.note: Covered to the whole hour only, and only to twenty o'clock, because the cardinals stop at twenty and no atom teaches minutes or the half and quarter forms.

points.label: 'day' as a unit, and 'now'
giving a date: this day of this month
points.note: Needs an ordinal or a number above twenty and a Gregorian month name; the track has none of the three.

points.label: asking somebody's age
answering with an age in years
points.note: The question was already taught at C19 and could not be answered. The tens, `samvatsaram` and the dative age frame together make the answer sayable.

points.label: before and after, ordering two events in time
points.note: Both ends now: `mundu` from C75 against `taruvaata` from C64.

points.label: identify oneself by name
ask somebody their name
ask what a thing is, or where a place is
give the standard personal information: name, age, where you are from
points.note: All three parts now: the name frame from C02, the age frame from C77, and origin from `nunci` with a place that has a name.

points.label: ask for confirmation with a tag: 'isn't it?'
confirm or deny what was just said
ask for an opinion by handing the turn back
give an opinion: 'I think that...'
ask for an evaluation: 'how is it?'
evaluate something as good, or as going well
express approval: that is fine
express disapproval
express agreement with what somebody said
express disagreement
points.note: `kaanii` supplies the 'but' this needed. The negative conjugation the note used to name as the other route also landed, at TE-GRAMMAR-C78-YESNO-03.

points.label: show scepticism, uncertainty or possibility: 'who knows'
offer a counter-argument
express certainty by plain assertion
ask whether somebody knows something
say that you know something
say that you do not know something
ask whether somebody can do something
say that you can do something, or have a skill
say what you like
ask about a preference by offering two alternatives
state a preference
say what you want or need
ask about somebody's plans
say what you are going to do
points.note: Carried by the -ta- piece, which C32 states covers 'I will go' as well as 'I go'.

points.label: give an order or an instruction
ask for an object, softened
points.note: `dayaceesi tii` is the one transactional request the track teaches as a whole utterance.

points.label: ask for help
respond to a request or an instruction
grant permission
refuse permission
offer something, or invite somebody
accept an offer or an invitation
decline an offer
greet
respond to a greeting
the time-of-day greetings: morning, afternoon, evening, night
judge which greeting is everyday and which is formal or dated
points.note: The proxy has no A1 slot for register, and the track's strongest single stretch is exactly this: four pragmatics atoms that weigh each greeting's currency and grade the confidence of the sources behind the claim.

points.label: address somebody by name or title
introduce yourself, and respond to being introduced
introduce a third person: 'this is my friend'
points.note: Still blocked by TE-A1-DEM-03, for the script reason recorded there. The genitive half arrived at C79 (`sneehitudi`); the adnominal half cannot be written without a new glyph.

points.label: apologise
points.note: C09 declares no lexis atom, so the probe names the etymology and pragmatics atoms it does declare.

points.label: accept an apology, and answer thanks -- one word does both
thank
offer condolences
propose a toast
congratulate, or wish somebody well on an occasion
take leave
open a conversation and react
greet and answer within a running conversation
ask for a person: 'is X there?'
show that you are following what is said
say you did not understand, or ask for a repeat
ask somebody to be quiet
propose closing the conversation
be polite: the word for please, and the -andi ending that carries politeness day to day
points.note: C08's pragmatics atom is explicit that the standalone `dayaceesi` is formal and that everyday politeness rides on -andi. That distinction has no Spanish counterpart and is exactly what an examiner scores.

points.label: say that you speak Telugu
the courtesy formulas of a household visit: welcome, respects, a blessing
the script runs left to right, one syllable block at a time
a consonant letter carries a built-in short a
a vowel sign rides on the consonant and changes the vowel's quality and length
every vowel sign an everyday word needs
points.note: Ten of Telugu's twelve everyday vowel signs have a recognition lesson of their own. The two that do not are the o and oo signs, and both are used by the track's own pages -- the oo sign 211 times and the o sign 144, counted over the 301 lesson files -- in roju, nooru, gooda, koodi, dooma and bhoojanam among others. See the scope note for why this is not a contradiction of the script-closure gate.

points.label: the ten vowel signs that do have a lesson
the virama, and the conjunct that stacks one consonant under the next
the anusvara for a word-final nasal
the independent vowel letters, for a vowel that starts a word
points.note: Four have a recognition lesson: i, u, e and vocalic r. Of the twelve that telugu/pronunciation-reference.md sets out, nine have none -- including `a` and `aa`, the two commonest, and `ee`, `o`, `oo` and `ai`. `a` alone is used 248 times across the track's own pages.

points.label: the four independent vowel letters that do have a lesson
the consonant letters, as a set a reader can finish a page with
points.note: Twenty-three of about thirty-six have a recognition lesson. Of the thirteen that do not, seven are used by the track's own pages and were counted there: ma 636 times, ta 292, ba 169, sha 105, dha 100, ssa 59 and pha 4. `ma` is in the very first word the book teaches, namaskaaram.

points.label: the twenty-three consonant letters that do have a lesson
the retroflex series, which Telugu spells out and English does not distinguish
points.note: dda, ddha and nna have recognition lessons; ta and tha do not. Retroflex ta is used 292 times across the track's pages -- in eemiti, maatlaadu, ganta, paata and baata, every one of them taught as a word.

points.label: the aspirate pairs Telugu writes with separate letters
spelling a word out syllable by syllable
the alphabet in its traditional order, and the names of the letters
points.note: Letters are introduced in the order words happen to need them, which is deliberate. Nothing gives the varnamaala order or the letter names, which is what dictating a spelling requires.

points.label: the full stop
points.note: No atom addresses punctuation at all. Telugu today writes the Latin full stop, and older text uses the danda; the track does not say which the reader should expect.

points.label: the comma
the question mark and the exclamation mark, written once at the end
points.note: Spanish's demand includes its inverted opening marks, which have no Telugu counterpart; the closing marks do transfer and are still not taught.

points.label: the colon, parentheses and quotation marks
the hyphen, the dash and the slash
abbreviations, initialisms and acronyms
symbols: the rupee sign, and reading a written price
reading the Telugu digits off a sign or a price ticket
points.note: Covered as recognition. Whether a candidate meets Telugu digits in the wild is a separate question this file does not answer.

points.label: the vowel length contrast, which distinguishes words
points.note: The track carries a `sounds:` list in every lesson's front matter and a whole pronunciation-reference.md, and NEITHER is an atom, so no probe can reach either. Every point in this category is unmapped for that one structural reason and not because the material is absent.

points.label: retroflex against dental consonants
aspirated against unaspirated stops
points.note: pronunciation-reference.md states the contrast in prose. No lesson declares an atom for it.

points.label: the anusvara's nasal, and where it assimilates
geminate consonants against single ones
word stress
the intonation that separates a statement from a question
points.note: Half of the obstacle is gone: the yes-or-no question the intonation would apply to is now taught (TE-A1-Q-08, C78). The point stays unmapped for the reason the whole category does -- the track declares no phonology atom anywhere, so no probe can reach the intonation itself.

points.label: existence and non-existence
stating a general quality of something
locating an event in time: the meeting is on Monday
points.note: The weekday names are taught (C10) and nothing lets a candidate attach one to an event -- no locative on a time word, no verb of appointment.

points.label: certainty and uncertainty as lexical items
relative position: near, far, right, left, in the middle
points.note: None of the five is introduced. A candidate who is told `ekkada?` cannot answer with anything but ikkada or akkada.

points.label: distance
movement and rest: go, come, sit, stand
orientation and direction
order: first, next, last
points.note: C75's `mundu` gives `before` and C64's `taruvaata` gives `after`, which closed TE-A1-T-10. Ordinal position -- first, next, last -- still needs the ordinals of TE-A1-NUM-04, which are absent.

points.label: origin: saying which place you are from
visibility and sight
audibility and hearing
colour
points.note: Six colours across two chapters. C22 declares only etymology atoms, so the probe names one of those.

points.label: age and old age as a property of a person
points.note: `paata` (C42) is explicitly glossed 'old -- of a thing, not of a person', so the track states the gap itself.

points.label: accessibility: open and closed, the way in and the way out
points.note: `talupu` (door) and `gadapa` (threshold) are taught as nouns; no verb opens or closes either.

points.label: general evaluation: good, bad, so-so
points.note: `ceddaa` closes the pair `manci` opened in C42. 'So-so' is still not a single word, but the good/bad axis the point turns on is now sayable at both ends.

points.label: value and price
attractiveness: handsome, pretty, ugly
saying a thing is a good one
acceptability: that will do
conformity: agreed, just so
correctness: that is true
ease and difficulty
reflection and knowledge: think, understand, know
verbal expression: speak, read, write, ask
parts of the body
points.note: Sixteen body-part atoms across five chapters -- far past what A1 asks, and one of the clearest places the track overshoots the level rather than missing it.

points.label: physical characteristics: tall, short, thin, fat
actions and positions of the body
character and personality adjectives
personal data: surname, address, telephone number
points.note: Only `peeru` exists. Every A1 writing paper is a form, and no field on one beyond the name can be filled.

points.label: documents: passport, identity card, ticket
personal objects
family relationships
points.note: Thirteen atoms including the age-graded sibling set and the affinal terms, which is well past A1 and is the track's other clear overshoot.

points.label: friend, and guest
the other social relations: colleague, neighbour, boss
the objects of a household occasion: a garland, a doorstep design, a blessing
the names of the festivals and family occasions themselves
the word for a meal
the meals of the day: breakfast, lunch, dinner
drink
points.note: C15 declares only etymology atoms, so water is probed through one of those.

points.label: foodstuffs
the taste words
points.note: The full five-taste set the Indian food vocabulary turns on. No Spanish A1 slot asks for it.

points.label: dishes and courses
the restaurant: ordering, the bill, the waiter
points.note: `dayaceesi tii` (C39) is the only transactional food utterance, and nothing around it -- no bill, no price question, no ordering frame.

points.label: educational institutions
teaching staff and students
the timetable, the examination and the marks
learning and studying
classroom language: look, listen, write, sit
teaching materials and classroom furniture
professions and posts
tools and the place of work
points.note: The tools are an axe, a saw, a spade, a hammer and a stick, and the workplace is a field. That is a village working life, which is a real answer to the proxy's demand and not the office one a city A1 paper would set.

points.label: working activity
unemployment and looking for work
rights and obligations at work
what makes a good worker
free time and entertainment
points.note: Nothing in the whole track names a leisure activity, which is the domain most A1 speaking prompts choose.

points.label: shows and exhibitions
sport
games
information and communication media
written correspondence: a letter, a message, an address
points.note: `kaburu` (C68) is oral news, which is the nearest the track comes.

points.label: the telephone
the printed press
television and radio
the internet, and dictating an e-mail address
buying, selling or renting a dwelling
the parts of a dwelling
the word for a house or a home
points.note: The wall, the roof, the threshold, the step, the window and the door are each taught and `illu` is not. Saying where you live needs the noun, not its parts.

points.label: domestic activities: cooking, cleaning, washing
points.note: `ciipuru` (a broom) is the only trace, and it is a noun.

points.label: household objects and furniture
the postal service
financial services
health services: the hospital, the clinic, the appointment
points.note: `vaidyudu` (a doctor) is taught and no place to find one is.

points.label: protection and security services
the places and people of shopping
clothing, footwear and accessories
points.note: `batta` ('cloth', C46) is the only textile word, and no garment is named.

points.label: paying: the currency, and the verb
points.note: `dabbu` (money) and `dhara` (price) are taught; there is no word for a rupee and no verb for paying, so the price turn cannot be completed.

points.label: health and illness
centres of health care
medicine and medicines
hygiene
travel objects and documents
setting out on a journey
accommodation
the transport system: the vehicles and the station
points.note: `baata` (a path) is the only word in the domain. No bus, train, ticket or stop.

points.label: money as a notion
commerce: the buyer and the seller
businesses and organisations
industry and energy
computing and new technology
political institutions and government
law and justice
artistic disciplines
music and dance
points.note: `paata` (a song, C68) is the only word, and neither the art nor the verb for performing it is named.

points.label: architecture, sculpture and painting
literature
photography
cinema and theatre
religion: the lamp, the garland, the doorstep design, the blessing
the universe and space
geography: the country, the town, the city, the capital
points.note: Two of the four named. C77 adds `pattanam` (town) and `deesam` (country) to C55's `graamam` (village); `nagaram` (city) and `raajadhaani` (capital) are still absent, and a point needs all of what it names.

points.label: rural space: the village, the field, the tank, the path
points.note: The rural half of the proxy's point is well covered and the urban half has nothing at all -- no street, no shop front beyond `angadi`, no building.

points.label: climate and weather
points.note: C20's grammar atom teaches `varsham padutoondi`, which is the one full weather sentence the track can produce.

points.label: fauna
flora
natural materials: sand, mud, fire
farming and the harvest
points.note: The proxy's industry slot has no A1 answer in Telugu here; what the track teaches instead is the agricultural cycle, on its own merits.

points.label: sounds and the voice
the abstract courtesy nouns: gratitude, respect, manners, trust
points.note: Six abstract nouns of courtesy, which is above A1 in register and taught anyway. Level purity is not a constraint on this curriculum, so they are recorded as coverage rather than as overshoot.
